items.bodyEn: Walking toward Kyoto, you keep Fuji on your right. Yoshiwara, the fourteenth post town, is the exception. Storm tides wrecked the town in 1639 and 1680, and each time it moved inland; the road that followed it bends so sharply that Fuji briefly appears on the left. Hiroshige drew three riders on one horse enjoying this Hidari Fuji.
items.sourceNote: Hiroshige, Yoshiwara: Left Fuji (1833–34); Dai Nihon Chimei Jisho (1900–07)

items.titleEn: Snow on Fuji, from Tago Bay
items.bodyEn: This stretch of Suruga Bay is Tago no Ura, named in one of Japan's best-known poems. Yamabe no Akahito, writing in the early 700s, came out onto the shore and saw snow falling on the white summit of Fuji. The version every schoolchild learns is the fourth poem of the Hyakunin Isshu; the original stands in the Man'yōshū.
items.ja: {田子|たご}の{浦|うら}にうち{出|い}でてみれば{白妙|しろたえ}の{富士|ふじ}の{高嶺|たかね}に{雪|ゆき}は{降|ふ}りつつ
items.kana: たごのうらにうちいでてみればしろたえのふじのたかねにゆきはふりつつ
items.sourceNote: Ogura Hyakunin Isshu no. 4 (Yamabe no Akahito); Man'yōshū, book 3

items.bodyEn: 左 and 右 both began as pictures of a hand, one left, one right. Later a tool, 工, was placed under the left hand and a mouth, 口, under the right. The two still begin differently when you write them: 左 starts with the horizontal stroke, 右 with the falling stroke, even though the finished characters look alike.
items.sourceNote: Shuowen Jiezi, entries 左 (hand + 工) and 右 (hand + 口)

items.bodyEn: Textbooks give the potential of Group 2 verbs as 〜られる: たべられる, みられる. In speech most people drop the ra: たべれる, みれる, これる. This ra-nuki form is marked wrong in formal writing and exams, but it has a real advantage: 〜られる can also be passive or honorific, while たべれる can only mean can eat. Recognize both; write the long one.
items.ja: {食|た}べられる・{食|た}べれる
items.kana: たべられる・たべれる
